question.text:
How can we best describe the following matrix?

\[ C = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Notice that $C$ is a matrix for which all entries above the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ C = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & \color{blue}0 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, it is a lower triangular matrix.

It is not an upper triangular matrix or a diagonal matrix since there is a non-zero element below the diagonal: $c_{21}=-5 \neq 0.$

question.text:
How can we best describe the following matrix?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is a matrix for which all entries above the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} 7 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 \\ 3 & -1 & \color{blue}0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, it is a lower triangular matrix.

It is not an upper triangular matrix or a diagonal matrix since there is a non-zero element below the diagonal: $a_{21}=3 \neq 0.$

question.text:
How can we best describe the following matrix?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 10 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is a matrix for which all entries below the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 10 & 1 \\ \color{blue}0 & 2 & 3 \\ \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, it is an upper triangular matrix.

It is not a lower triangular matrix or a diagonal matrix since there is a non-zero element above the diagonal: $a_{12}=10 \neq 0.$

question.text:
How can we best describe the following matrix?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is a matrix for which all entries above and below the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 \\ \color{blue}0 & 5 & \color{blue}0 \\ \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, it is a diagonal matrix.

question.text:
How can we best describe the following matrix?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is a matrix for which all entries above and below the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 \\ \color{blue}0 & 3 & \color{blue}0 \\ \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, it is a diagonal matrix.

question.text: Which of the following is an upper triangular matrix?
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is a matrix for which all entries below the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Hence, it is an upper triangular matrix.

By contrast, matrices $B$, $C$, $D$, and $E$ each have at least one non-zero entry below the diagonal:

\[ B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}-5} & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}-1} & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}1} & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \quad E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}1} & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, they are not upper triangular matrices.

question.text:
Which of the following matrices are upper triangular matrices?

$ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.65 & 1 & 8\\ 0 & 2 & 3 & 0.89 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 9.87 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
The matrices $B$ and $C$ are upper triangular matrices since all the entries below the main diagonal are zeros.

The matrix $A$ is not an upper triangular matrix since it has a non-zero element below the main diagonal: \begin{align} a_{43} &= 1 \neq 0 \end{align}

question.text: Which of the following is a lower triangular matrix?
question.explanation:
Notice that $B$ is a matrix for which all entries above the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} \\ 2 & 5 & {\color{blue}0} \\ 1 & 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \] Hence, it is a lower triangular matrix.

By contrast, matrices $A$, $C$, $D$, and $E$ each have at least one non-zero entry above the diagonal:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}1}\\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}1} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}-3} \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad E = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}-4} & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -7 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, they are not lower triangular matrices.

question.text: Which of the following is an upper triangular matrix?
question.explanation:
Notice that $D$ is a matrix for which all entries below the diagonal are $0$'s: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 6 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & 1 & -1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 2 \end{bmatrix} \] Hence, it is an upper triangular matrix.

By contrast, matrices $A$, $B$, $C$, and $E$ each have at least one non-zero entry below the diagonal:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}1} & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}2} & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}5} & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad E = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\color{red}4} & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, they are not upper triangular matrices.

question.text:
Which of the following matrices are upper triangular matrices?

$ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
The matrix $A$ is an upper triangular matrix since all the entries below the main diagonal are zeros.

The matrices $B$ and $C$ are not upper triangular matrices since they each have a non-zero element below the main diagonal: \begin{align} b_{21} &= 2 \neq 0 \\ c_{32} &= -2 \neq 0 \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Correct Statements About a Matrix

question.text:
Consider the matrix $A= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 & -7 \\ 2 & -1 & 8 \\ 7 & -8 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $A$ is upper triangular
  2. $A$ is lower triangular
  3. $A+A^T$ is upper triangular
question.explanation:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is false, since $A$ has non-zero entries below the main diagonal: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 & -7 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}2}} & -1 & 8 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}7}} & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}-8}} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement II is false, since $A$ has non-zero entries above the main diagonal: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}-2}} & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}-7}} \\ 2 & -1 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}8}} \\ 7 & -8 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement III is true, since the result of $A+A^T$ has all the entries below the main diagonal equal to zero: \[ A+A^T=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & -2 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

question.text:
Consider the matrix $D= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $D$ is upper triangular
  2. $D$ is lower triangular
  3. $D^T$ is upper triangular
question.explanation:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is false, since $D$ has non-zero entries below the main diagonal: \[ D=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} & 3 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement II is true. All the entries above the main diagonal of $D$ are zeros: \[ D=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} \\ 0 & 2 & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & {\color{blue}0} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement III is true. All the entries below the main diagonal of $D^T$ are zeros: \[ D^T=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 3 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 4 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only".

question.text:
Consider the matrix $B= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $B$ is upper triangular
  2. $B$ is lower triangular
  3. $B^T+B$ is upper triangular
question.explanation:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is false, since $B$ has non-zero entries below the main diagonal: \[ B=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}5}} & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}-2}} & -4 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement II is false, since $B$ has non-zero entries above the main diagonal: \[ B=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}-5}} \\ 0 & 2& \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}2}} \\ 5 & -2 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement III is true, since the result of $B^T+B$ has all the entries below the main diagonal equal to zero: \[ B^T+B=\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & 4 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & -8 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

question.text:
Consider the matrix $A= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $A$ is upper triangular
  2. $A$ is lower triangular
  3. $A^T$ is lower triangular
question.explanation:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is false, since $A$ has non-zero entries below the main diagonal: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 &\bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red} 1 }}& 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement II is false, since $A$ has non-zero entries above the main diagonal: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}-3}} & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 &1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement III is false, since $A^T$ has non-zero entries above the main diagonal: \[ A^T=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} & 0\\ -3 & 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "None".

  1. $D$ is upper triangular
  2. $D$ is lower triangular
  3. $D^T$ is upper triangular
question.explanation:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is false, since $D$ has non-zero entries below the main diagonal: \[ D=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{{\color{red}1}} & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement II is true. All the entries above the main diagonal of $D$ are zeros: \[ D=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & {\color{blue} 0 } & {\color{blue} 0 } \\ 0 & 2 & {\color{blue} 0 } \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Statement III is true. All the entries below the main diagonal of $D^T$ are zeros: \[ D^T=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue} 0 } & 2 & 0 \\ {\color{blue} 0 } & {\color{blue} 0 } & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only".
